 Ranbir Kapoor Films: Five Roles, Five Box Office Outcomes 
Mumbai | 15 Nov, 2026 | 12:43 PM IST | By DPIFF Editorial Desk | Share 
 Share this link via
 Ranbir Kapoor Films: Five Roles, Five Box Office Outcomes
 Ranbir Kapoor’s recent theatrical run offers a revealing look at the range, risks and uneven outcomes that can shape a contemporary Hindi film career. A recent DPIFF Instagram post brings together five films— Animal , Sanju , Tu Jhoothi Main Makkaar , Brahmāstra and Shamshera —to examine how the actor has moved between intense drama, romance, fantasy spectacle and period action.
 The films represent markedly different creative choices as well as contrasting box office verdicts. Animal emerged as an All-Time Blockbuster, while Rajkumar Hirani’s Sanju achieved blockbuster status. Tu Jhoothi Main Makkaar found a sizeable audience, whereas Brahmāstra and Shamshera faced different challenges in translating ambition and scale into theatrical success.
 Five films, five different career conversations
 What makes this group significant is not simply the difference between successful and underperforming releases. Together, the films show Ranbir Kapoor repeatedly choosing projects that demand a change in tone, physicality and performance style.
 In Sanju , Kapoor took on the difficult task of portraying actor Sanjay Dutt across several stages of his life. The film required him to communicate not only physical resemblance but also shifts in vulnerability, confidence and emotional conflict. Its success established the biographical drama as one of the defining milestones of his career.
 Animal marked a much more confrontational turn. Directed by Sandeep Reddy Vanga, the film placed Kapoor in an intensely volatile world and generated substantial discussion around its themes, relationships and presentation of masculinity. Regardless of how individual viewers respond to the film, its scale of audience engagement made it a major theatrical event. The film’s production and cast details also reflect the size of the project Kapoor chose to lead.
 With Tu Jhoothi Main Makkaar , Kapoor returned to the romantic-comedy space. Directed by Luv Ranjan, the film paired him with Shraddha Kapoor and relied on relationship dynamics, family situations and contemporary urban humour. Its performance demonstrated that Kapoor could continue to connect with audiences outside the darker and more dramatic territory associated with some of his later roles.
 Ambition, scale and the risks of spectacle
 Brahmāstra: Part One – Shiva represented a different kind of career move. Directed by Ayan Mukerji, the film attempted to establish a large-scale fantasy universe rooted in Indian mythology and popular visual culture. Kapoor played Shiva, an ordinary young man drawn into a supernatural conflict, making the film an ambitious experiment in franchise-led Hindi cinema.
 The project’s importance extends beyond its commercial verdict. It showed the growing willingness of mainstream Hindi filmmakers to invest in original fantasy worlds rather than rely exclusively on established comic-book properties or remakes. At the same time, films built around visual effects and expansive world-building face a higher level of expectation from audiences. Brahmāstra’s film record provides useful context for understanding that creative and industrial ambition.
 Shamshera presented another demanding challenge: a period action drama built around rebellion, identity and spectacle. Kapoor played a double role in the film, which sought to combine a historical setting with the scale of a mainstream action entertainer. Its difficult box office run illustrates how production scale alone cannot guarantee audience connection. Narrative clarity, timing, positioning and word of mouth remain equally important in determining a film’s theatrical journey.
 Why the comparison matters
 Looking at these five films together avoids reducing an actor’s career to a single success or failure. Kapoor’s recent choices show a willingness to move between genres rather than remain within one dependable screen image. That approach carries creative rewards, but it also exposes an actor to more varied audience responses.
 The comparison is particularly relevant in an industry where box office performance often becomes the first measure of a film’s value. Commercial outcomes matter to the theatrical ecosystem, but they do not fully explain the artistic or cultural significance of a project. Sanju remains notable for its biographical performance challenge; Brahmāstra for its attempt to create a home-grown fantasy franchise; and Shamshera for the scale of its period-action ambition.
 Likewise, the success of Animal and Tu Jhoothi Main Makkaar highlights the range of audience spaces Kapoor has been able to occupy. One film pursued an aggressive, adult-oriented dramatic identity, while the other worked within the conventions of the modern Hindi romantic comedy. Their contrast is central to understanding the actor’s recent theatrical journey.
 Ranbir Kapoor’s evolving screen identity
 Since his early career, Kapoor has often been associated with characters negotiating identity, relationships and emotional uncertainty. His recent filmography adds action, fantasy, biography and morally complex drama to that screen identity. The result is a career shaped less by one fixed persona than by the actor’s willingness to test different formats.
 The five-film comparison also invites a broader question about how audiences assess performers. Is an actor at their best when a film becomes a blockbuster, when a performance demands transformation, or when the role reveals a new dimension? There is no single answer, and that is precisely why the discussion remains engaging.
